extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, classical geometers, and mathematicians interested in Archimedean methods
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying historical methods used (in Archimedes and later commentators) for (1) generating rational/integer solutions of x^2 - a y^2 = const (Pell-type Diophantine methods) to obtain successive approximations to square roots, and (2) solving neusis (νεῦσις) geometric problems including reductions of angle-trisection and cube-duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theon’s rule of formation (side- and diagonal-numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theon of Smyrna’s recurrence giving side- and diagonal-numbers which produce successive approximations to √2; the rule generates sequences of integers (side-numbers a_n and diagonal-numbers d_n) such that successive fractions d_n/a_n approximate √2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents Theon’s recurrence and shows how d_n^2 − 2 a_n^2 = ±1 alternates, so d_n/a_n converges to √2. Use the recurrence to produce arbitrarily many approximations; the method historically underlies the Pythagorean/‘diagonal-side’ system and is linked to Plato’s references to rational/irrational diagonals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Pell-type equation x^2 − a y^2 = ±1 to generate approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate successive rational/integer approximations to √a by finding integer solutions of x^2 − a y^2 = ±1 (or other small constants). Solutions produce convergents x/y approximating √a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one (nontrivial) solution is known, algebraic identities and substitution formulas allow generation of infinitely many further solutions; this is the general principle behind many historical methods treated (for a=2 and a=3 in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeuthen’s substitution method for a=3
rubrics_metrics.description: Use substitutions (derived from Euclid II.5 identities) to produce an identity and a recurrence that transforms one solution of m^2 − 3 n^2 = 1 into another; starting from m=2, n=1 one obtains a sequence (2,1) → (7,4) → (26,15) … giving approximations to √3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the explicit algebraic identity (given in the exposition) and the multiplication-up trick to compute next solutions; the method treats both equations x^2 − 3y^2 = 1 and x^2 − 3y^2 = −2 together to produce the Archimedean approximations to √3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tannery’s first (Diophantine) method
rubrics_metrics.description: A general method: given one integral solution (p,q) of x^2 − a y^2 = 1, assume linear forms for new solutions (p' = a p + b q, q' = c p + d q) and determine coefficients by solving linear systems, thereby producing further integral solutions; can be applied to x^2 − a y^2 = r as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tannery’s formulation shows how, from three simplest known solutions, one can determine the parameters a,b,c,d and generate subsequent solutions (examples provided for a=3 and for the companion equation x^2 − 3y^2 = −2). Method advantage: it extends to any x^2 − a y^2 = r.

rubrics_metrics.name: De Lagny’s near-equality search method
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for fractions whose numerator^2 differs as little as possible from 3 times the denominator^2 (or generally a times), producing two sequences of fractions one greater and one less than √a, with a simple linear recurrence between consecutive terms (e.g., p_next = 2p + 3q, q_next = p + 2q in the text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form consecutive relations by trial/computation of close integer squares; this yields two monotone sequences that converge to √a. Historically precedes and anticipates later Diophantine approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heilermann’s generalisation of Theon’s recurrence (Pellian recurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalise Theon’s side/diagonal recurrence by substituting arbitrary integer a in the second relation, producing recurrences S_n = S_{n−1} + D_{n−1}, D_n = a S_{n−1} + 2 D_{n−1}, and showing D_n^2 − a S_n^2 = (1−a)^n (D_0^2 − a S_0^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose initial S_0,D_0 appropriately (often small integers); where the right-hand fraction tends to zero as n increases, D_n/S_n approximates √a. For speed, choose auxiliary scaling b to make b^2 a near 1 (the text gives an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tannery’s second (series/approximation) method
rubrics_metrics.description: Form algebraic expressions for √(large number) as sums/continued-like expressions and, by squaring and neglecting negligible terms, obtain integral parts and successive approximations (used on large radicands and on √3 examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the root as a sum of integer terms plus small corrections, square, neglect higher-order (assumed small) pieces to obtain integer approximations, then refine using first-method generation of more exact solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rodet, Oppermann, Schénborn and related ad hoc methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Various historical one-off formulae and manipulations that produce some Archimedean approximations (Rodet for particular examples; Oppermann and Schénborn producing one of the Archimedean approximations or near the Hunrath–Hultsch formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods are generally less systematic; they may yield isolated approximations or reproduce known ones but are typically superseded by the Diophantine/Pell-style recurrences or Tannery’s methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using two companion indeterminate equations to capture both adjacent approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover the two sequences of Archimedean approximations to √a (greater and lesser), treat simultaneously the two equations x^2 − a y^2 = 1 and x^2 − a y^2 = −2 (or other companion constants) and use identities linking them to produce paired sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As applied to √3 in the text: solving x^2 − 3 y^2 = 1 and x^2 − 3 y^2 = −2 together yields both series of convergents that Archimedes’ approximations occupy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of νεῦσις (neusis) problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A line is said to 'verge' (νεύειν) towards a point if, when produced, it reaches the point. A νεῦσις problem: given two lines/curves and a fixed point, draw between them a straight line (passing through the fixed point) whose intercept between the two given lines/curves has a prescribed length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly: the required line must pass through the given point and the segment intercepted between the two given lines/curves must be exactly the prescribed length. This is the geometric object reduced in many classical constructions (trisection, mean proportionals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic reduction and solvability conditions for a general νεῦσις
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting coordinates (taking O origin, etc.) reduces the general νεῦσις to algebraic equations: generically a quartic in the unknown intercept parameter, or to a coupled system for auxiliary variables; special cases reduce to quadratics solvable by application of areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: with OD=a, AD=b, BC=2c the relations lead after rationalisation to a quartic; if A is endpoint of the diameter bisecting BC (a=0) the problem reduces to a quadratic solvable geometrically by application of areas. Use algebraic reduction to identify whether classical 'plane' methods suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of problems: plane, solid, and linear
rubrics_metrics.description: Pappus’ classification: plane problems are solvable by a straight line and a circle (plane constructions); solid problems require conic sections; linear problems require more intricate curves (spirals, quadratrices, conchoids, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining how to attempt a problem, first test whether it admits a plane solution; if not, conics or linear curves (or mechanical constructions) are legitimate classical devices. Pappus views solving by a 'foreign' kind (e.g., conics for a plane problem) as an error, but the text defends Archimedes where only the possibility of a solution was assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conics to solve 'solid' νεύσεις and to determine διορισμός
rubrics_metrics.description: Solving a 'solid' νεῦσις via intersections of conics (parabola/hyperbola, etc.) enables not only a construction but also the determination of the διορισμός (the criterion/limits for the real possibility and the number of solutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conic intersections give effective algebraic control: e.g., translating the geometric constraints to a hyperbola and a parabola; the maximal admissible intercept length k corresponds to tangency of the two curves. Apollonius’ conic theory is presented as well-suited to such analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical constructions as legitimate substitutes for conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical devices and ruler-and-mark constructions were historically accepted substitutes for constructing and effecting neusis solutions when conics were difficult to draw; moving a marked ruler through the fixed point until the second mark hits the second curve is an allowable procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Apollonius’ and Philo’s mechanical constructions for mean proportionals; Philo Byzantinus’ ruler-moving solution; such mechanical processes can be viewed as generating intersections with an implicitly defined curve (often a rectangular hyperbola or conchoid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conchoid method (Nicomedes) for neusis with a straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: When one of the two given lines is a straight line, construct Nicomedes’ conchoid with the fixed point as pole and the given length as the conchoid’s distance; intersections of the given curve with this conchoid provide the required intercepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conchoid has polar equation r = a + b secθ (pole at fixed point). Historically one could either draw the conchoid or simply move a ruler with marks until the intercept equals the given length; the conchoid solves all such neusis instances where one curve is straight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of duplication of the cube to a νεῦσις
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the problem of finding two mean proportionals (equivalently doubling the cube) to a νεῦσις: place a line through a fixed point with intercept equal to a prescribed length (obtained by an auxiliary construction), then use parallels and Euclid’s results to show constructed segments are the desired mean proportionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the sequence in the text: set up rectangle/parallelogram, reduce to a neusis of intercept equal to a constructed length (e.g., AD), solve the neusis (e.g., via conchoid), then recover mean proportionals via parallels and similarity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of angle-trisection to a νεῦσις (and solution by conics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce trisecting an angle to a νεῦσις: construct a rectangle/parallelogram and require a line through a corner whose certain intercept equals a given multiple of a side; the auxiliary point then lies at intersection of a circle and a rectangular hyperbola — intersection yields solution and hence trisection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction: given rectangle ABCD and required intercept QA = k, the locus of the auxiliary point P is both a circle (center D radius k) and a rectangular hyperbola (BR, BA as asymptotes). Their intersection yields P; from P recover the line that effects trisection. This shows how conics/hyperbolas are naturally implicated in trisection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus’ lemmas on loci (hyperbola and parabola)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 1: If from a fixed point A any line meets a fixed line BC and if RQ is drawn perpendicular to BC bearing a given ratio to AA, the locus of Q is a hyperbola. Lemma 2: If BC has given length, and from a point R on BC a perpendicular RY is drawn such that BR·RC = k·RY, the locus of Q is a parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lemmas provide the geometric loci used to reduce neusis to conic intersections. In coordinates they correspond to equations of a rectangular hyperbola and a parabola; use them to convert neusis geometric conditions to conic equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diορισμός (criterion/limits for solution) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any complete solution should be accompanied by a διορισμός — i.e., the criterion showing when a real solution is possible and giving the number/limits of solutions (e.g., the maximal intercept length k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, after reducing the geometry to intersection of curves, compute the parameter ranges for which intersections are real (tangency gives maximal admissible k). Apollonius’ conic theory (or Zeuthen’s hyperbola/parabola intersection analysis) is recommended to compute the διορισμός.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane special cases where neusis reduces to circle/line constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify configurations (e.g., B on the angle bisector so parallelogram AC'BD is a rhombus or square) where the general neusis simplifies to a plane problem solvable by straight line and circle only (no conics needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test geometric symmetry conditions: if the auxiliary hyperbola degenerates or the parameter choices make algebraic degree drop (e.g., quartic→quadratic), use classical Euclidean 'application of areas' constructions or circle/line methods instead of conics.
